r) = 9 and a^2/(1 - r^2) = 81/5.
Dividing: a/(1 + r) = 9/5, so a = (9/5)(1 + r). With a

= 9(1 - r) this gives 9(1 - r) = (9/5)(1 + r), i.e.
5 - 5r = 1 + r, so r = 2/3 and a = 3.

Hence the series is 3 + 2 + 4/3 + 8/9 + ...

mcqs.q: What is the sum of the first 15 terms of 1, 1/3, 1/9, ... ?
What is the correct sum to n terms of .2 + .22 + .222 + ... ?
mcqs.why: Each term is 2 x (1 - 10^(-k))/9, and 1/10 + ... + 1/10^n = (1/9)(1 - 1/10^n). Sum = (2/9)[n - (1/9)(1 - 1/10^n)]. The printed key appears to read 1/n; the notes flag the correct factor as 1/9.

mcqs.q: What is the sum to infinity of 1/5 + 1/25 + 1/125 + ... ?
What is the sum to infinity of 9/4 + 3/2 + 1 + 2/3 + ... ?
What is the sum to infinity of 4 + 2 sqrt(2) + 2 + sqrt(2) + 1 + ... ?
mcqs.why: a = 4, r = sqrt(2)/2: S = 4/(1 - sqrt(2)/2) = 8/(2 - sqrt(2)) = 4(2 + sqrt(2)) after rationalising.

mcqs.q: What vulgar fraction equals 0.777... ?
mcqs.why: 0.777... is the infinite G.P. 7/10 + 7/100 + ... with sum (7/10)/(1 - 1/10) = 7/9, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What vulgar fraction equals 1.3434... ?
A ball dropped from 27 m rebounds two-thirds of the distance it falls each time. What total distance does it travel before coming to rest?
A ball dropped from 75 m rebounds 2/5 of the distance it fell each time. What total distance does it travel before coming to rest?
The sum of an infinite G.P. is 9 and the sum of the squares of its terms is 81/5. What is the series?

lessons.title: Exercise 6.9
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-6

1. A man deposits in a bank Rs. 8 in the first year, Rs. 24 in the second year, Rs. 72

in the third year and so on. Find the amount he will have deposited in the bank by

the fifth year. 2. A man borrows Rs. 32760 without interest and agrees to repay the

loan in installments, each installment being twice the preceding one. Find the

amount of the last installment, if the amount of the first installment is Rs. 8. 3. The

population of a certain village is 62500. What will be its population after 3 years if it

increases geometrically at the rate of 4% annually? 4. The enrollment of a famous

school doubled after every eight years from 1970 to 1994. If the enrollment was

6000 in 1994, what was its enrollment in 1970? 5. A singular cholera bacteria

produces two complete bacteria in 1/2 hours. If we start with a colony of A bacteria,

how many bacteria will we have in n hours? 6. Joining the mid points of the sides of

an equilateral triangle, an equilateral triangle having half the perimeter of the

original triangle is obtained. We form a sequence of nested equilateral triangles in

the manner described above with the original triangle having perimeter 3/2. What

will be the total perimeter of all the triangles formed in this way?

1.
The deposits form a G.P. with a = 8 and r = 3.
The total by the fifth year is S_5 =

8(3^5 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 4 x 242 = Rs. 968. 2.
The installments form a G.P. with a = 8

and r = 2.
If there are n installments, 8(2^n - 1) = 32760, so 2^n - 1 = 4095 and

2^n = 4096, giving n = 12.
The last installment is 8 x 2^11 = Rs. 16384. 3. The

population after 3 years is 62500 x (1.04)^3 = 62500 x 1.124864 = 70304. 4. From

1970 to 1994 is 24 years, i.e. three doublings.
So the 1970 enrollment was

6000/2^3 = 750. 5.
The bacteria double every half hour, so in n hours there are 2n

doublings.
Hence the number of bacteria is A x 2^(2n) = A x 4^n. 6. The perimeters

form a G.P. with a = 3/2 and r = 1/2.
The total perimeter is (3/2)/(1 - 1/2) = 3.

mcqs.q: Deposits of Rs. 8, Rs. 24, Rs. 72, ... form a G.P. What is its common ratio?
mcqs.why: r = 24/8 = 3, also 72/24 = 3, so the common ratio is 3.

mcqs.q: A man deposits Rs. 8, Rs. 24, Rs. 72, ... yearly. How much has he deposited by the fifth year?
Installments doubling each time, first Rs. 8, repay a loan of Rs. 32760. How many installments are there?
For the same loan (first installment Rs. 8, each double the preceding, 12 installments), what is the last installment?
mcqs.why: Last installment = 8 x 2^11 = 8 x 2048 = 16384 rupees.

mcqs.q: A village population is 62500 and increases geometrically at 4% annually. What is it after 3 years?
School enrollment doubled every eight years from 1970 to 1994 and was 6000 in 1994. What was it in 1970?
mcqs.why: 1970 to 1994 is 24 years = three doublings. 1970 enrollment = 6000/2^3 = 6000/8 = 750.

mcqs.q: A cholera bacteria produces two bacteria in 1/2 hour. How many doublings occur in n hours?
mcqs.why: Doubling every half hour means 2 doublings per hour, so in n hours there are 2n doublings, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Starting with a colony of A bacteria doubling every 1/2 hour, how many bacteria are there in n hours?
mcqs.why: With 2n doublings, number = A x 2^(2n) = A x (2^2)^n = A x 4^n.

mcqs.q: Nested equilateral triangles are formed from one with perimeter 3/2, each next having half the perimeter. What G.P. do the perimeters form?
What is the total perimeter of all the nested triangles with first perimeter 3/2 and ratio 1/2?
mcqs.why: Total = (3/2)/(1 - 1/2) = (3/2)/(1/2) = 3, using the infinite G.P. sum a/(1-r).

lessons.title: Exercise 6.10
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-5

1. Find the 9th term of the harmonic sequence i) 1/3, 1/5, 1/7, ... ii) -1/5, -1/3, -1, ...

2. Find the 12th terms of the following harmonic sequences i) 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, ... ii) 1/3,

2/9, 1/6, ... 3. Insert five harmonic means between the following given numbers, i)

-2/5 and 2/13 ii) 1/4 and 1/24 4. Insert four harmonic means between the following

given numbers. i) 1/3 and 1/23 ii) 7/3 and 7/11 iii) 4 and 20 5. If the 7th and 10th

terms of an H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21 respectively, find its 14th term.

1. i) The reciprocals 3, 5, 7, ... form an A.P. with d = 2, so the 9th reciprocal is 3 + 16

= 19 and the 9th term is 1/19. ii) The reciprocals -5, -3, -1, ... form an A.P. with d =

2, so the 9th reciprocal is -5 + 16 = 11 and the 9th term is 1/11.
2. i) The reciprocals

2, 5, 8, ... form an A.P. with d = 3, so the 12th reciprocal is 2 + 33 = 35 and the 12th

term is 1/35. ii) The reciprocals 3, 9/2, 6, ... form an A.P. with d = 3/2, so the 12th

reciprocal is 3 + 33/2 = 39/2 and the 12th term is 2/39.
3. i) The reciprocals are -5/2

and 13/2; with five means the A.P. has d = (13/2 + 5/2)/6 = 3/2, giving reciprocals

-5/2, -1, 1/2, 2, 7/2, 5, 13/2.
Hence the harmonic means are -1, 2, 1/2, 2/7, 1/5. ii)

The reciprocals are 4 and 24; with five means d = 20/6 = 10/3, giving reciprocals 4,

22/3, 32/3, 14, 52/3, 62/3, 24.
Hence the harmonic means are 3/22, 3/32, 1/14,

3/52, 3/62.
4. i) The reciprocals are 3 and 23; with four means d = 20/5 = 4, giving

reciprocals 7, 11, 15, 19.
Hence the harmonic means are 1/7, 1/11, 1/15, 1/19. ii)

The reciprocals are 3/7 and 11/7; with four means d = (8/7)/5 = 8/35, giving

reciprocals 23/35, 31/35, 39/35, 47/35.
Hence the harmonic means are 35/23,

35/31, 35/39, 35/47. iii) The reciprocals are 1/4 and 1/20; with four means d =

(-1/5)/5 = -1/25, giving reciprocals 21/100, 17/100, 13/100, 9/100. Hence the

harmonic means are 100/21, 100/17, 100/13, 100/9. 5.
The reciprocals of the 7th

and 10th terms are 3 and 21/5.
In the reciprocal A.P., a + 6d = 3 and a + 9d = 21/5,

so 3d = 6/5, i.e. d = 2/5, and a = 3 - 12/5 = 3/5.
The 14th reciprocal is 3/5 + 13 x

2/5 = 29/5, so the 14th term is 5/29.

Q6-11

6. The first term of an H.P. is -1/3 and the fifth term is 1/5. Find its 9th term. 7. If 5 is

the harmonic mean between 2 and b, find b. 8. If the numbers 1/k, 1/(2k + 1) and

1/(4k - 1) are in harmonic sequence, find k. 9. Find n so that (a^(n+1) +

b^(n+1))/(a^n + b^n) may be H.M. between a and b. 10. If a^2, b^2 and c^2 are

in A.P., show that a + b, c + a and b + c are in H.P. 11. The sum of the first and fifth

terms of the harmonic sequence is 4/7, if the first term is 1/2, find the sequence.

6.
The reciprocals form an A.P. with first term -3 and fifth term 5, so -3 + 4d = 5 and

d = 2.
The 9th reciprocal is -3 + 16 = 13, so the 9th term is 1/13. 7. The harmonic

mean is 2 x 2b/(2 + b) = 4b/(2 + b) = 5, so 4b = 10 + 5b and b = -10. 8. The

reciprocals k, 2k + 1, 4k - 1 are in A.P., so 2(2k + 1) = k + (4k - 1), i.e. 4k + 2 = 5k -

1, so k = 3.
FLAG: the printed key reads 'k = 67' for this part, but k = 67 does not

satisfy the A.P. condition (for k = 67 the reciprocals are 67, 135, 267, and 2 x 135 =

270 is not 67 + 267 = 334); the value forced by the condition is k = 3. 9. Setting

(a^(n+1) + b^(n+1))/(a^n + b^n) = 2ab/(a + b) gives (a + b)(a^(n+1) +

b^(n+1)) = 2ab(a^n + b^n), i.e. a^(n+2) - a^(n+1)b - ab^(n+1) + b^(n+2) = 0,

i.e.
(a - b)(a^(n+1) - b^(n+1)) = 0.
For a != b this gives a^(n+1) = b^(n+1), so n

+ 1 = 0 and n = -1. 10.
We need the reciprocals 1/(a + b), 1/(c + a), 1/(b + c) to be

in A.P., i.e.
2/(c + a) = 1/(a + b) + 1/(b + c) = (a + 2b + c)/((a + b)(b + c)), i.e. 2(a

+ b)(b + c) = (c + a)(a + c + 2b).
Expanding: the left side is 2ab + 2b^2 + 2ac +

2bc and the right side is a^2 + 2ac + c^2 + 2ab + 2bc.
The two sides are equal

exactly when a^2 + c^2 = 2b^2, which is the given A.P. condition. Hence a + b, c

+ a, b + c are in H.P., as required. 11.
The reciprocal A.P. has first term 2; the fifth

reciprocal is 2 + 4d, so the fifth term is 1/(2 + 4d).
Then 1/2 + 1/(2 + 4d) = 4/7, so

1/(2 + 4d) = 1/14, i.e.
2 + 4d = 14 and d = 3.
Hence the sequence is 1/2, 1/5, 1/8,

1/11, ...

Q12-13

12. If A, G and H are the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means between a and

b respectively, show that G^2 = A.H. 13. Find A, G, H and show that G^2 = A.H. if i)

a = -2, b = -6 ii) a = 2i, b = 4i iii) a = 9, b = 4 14.
Find A, G, H and verify that A > G

> H (G > 0), if i) a = 2, b = 8 ii) a = 2/5, b = 8/5 15.
Find A, G, H and verify that A <

G < H (G < 0), if i) a = -2, b = -8 ii) a = -2/5, b = -8/5

12.
Here A = (a + b)/2, G^2 = ab and H = 2ab/(a + b), so A.H = ab = G^2, as

required.
13. i) A = (-2 - 6)/2 = -4; G^2 = (-2)(-6) = 12, so G = +- sqrt(12); H =

2(12)/(-8) = -3.
Then A.H = (-4)(-3) = 12 = G^2. ii) A = (2i + 4i)/2 = 3i; G^2 =

(2i)(4i) = -8; H = 2(-8)/(6i) = 8i/3.
Then A.H = 3i x 8i/3 = -8 = G^2. FLAG: the

printed key writes 'G = -8' for this part, but -8 is G^2, not G (G = 2 sqrt(2) i, taking

the principal square root). iii) A = (9 + 4)/2 = 13/2; G^2 = 36, so G = +- 6; H =

2(36)/13 = 72/13.
Then A.H = (13/2)(72/13) = 36 = G^2.
14. i) A = 5, G = 4, H =

16/5 = 3.2, so 5 > 4 > 3.2, i.e.
A > G > H. ii) A = 1, G = 4/5, H = 16/25 = 0.64, so 1

> 0.8 > 0.64, i.e.
A > G > H. 15. i) A = -5, G = -4 (the negative square root, since G

< 0), H = -16/5 = -3.2, so -5 < -4 < -3.2, i.e.
A < G < H. ii) A = -1, G = -4/5, H =

-16/25 = -0.64, so -1 < -0.8 < -0.64, i.e. A < G < H.

16.
If the H.M. and A.M. between two numbers are 4 and 9/2 respectively, find the

numbers. 17.
If the (positive) G.M. and H.M. between two numbers are 4 and 16/5,

find the numbers. 18.
If the numbers 1/2, 4/21 and 1/36 are subtracted from the

three consecutive terms of a G.P., the resulting numbers are in H.P. Find the

numbers if their product is 1/27.

16.
Let the numbers be x and y: x + y = 9 and 2xy/(x + y) = 4, so xy = 18. Hence x

and y are the roots of t^2 - 9t + 18 = (t - 6)(t - 3) = 0, so the numbers are 6 and 3.

17.
Let the numbers be x and y: xy = 16 and 2xy/(x + y) = 16/5, so x + y = 10.

Hence x and y are the roots of t^2 - 10t + 16 = (t - 8)(t - 2) = 0, so the numbers are

8 and 2. 18.
Let the G.P. terms be a/r, a, ar: their product is a^3 = 1/27, so a = 1/3.

After subtracting: 1/(3r) - 1/2, 1/3 - 4/21 = 1/7, r/3 - 1/36 are in H.P., so their

reciprocals are in A.P.: 2 x 7 = 6r/(2 - 3r) + 36/(12r - 1).
Solving: 14(2 - 3r)(12r - 1) =

6r(12r - 1) + 36(2 - 3r), i.e.
144r^2 - 123r + 25 = 0, i.e.
(3r - 1)(48r - 25) = 0, so r =

1/3 or r = 25/48.
For r = 1/3 the numbers are 1, 1/3, 1/9; for r = 25/48 the numbers

are 16/25, 1/3, 25/144.

mcqs.q: What is the 9th term of the harmonic sequence 1/3, 1/5, 1/7, ... ?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals 3, 5, 7, ... form an A.P. with d = 2. 9th reciprocal = 3 + 8(2) = 19, so 9th term = 1/19.

mcqs.q: What is the 9th term of the harmonic sequence -1/5, -1/3, -1, ... ?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals -5, -3, -1, ... form an A.P. with d = 2. 9th reciprocal = -5 + 8(2) = 11, so 9th term = 1/11.

mcqs.q: What is the 12th term of the harmonic sequence 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, ... ?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals 2, 5, 8, ... form an A.P. with d = 3. 12th reciprocal = 2 + 11(3) = 35, so 12th term = 1/35.

mcqs.q: What is the 12th term of the harmonic sequence 1/3, 2/9, 1/6, ... ?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals 3, 9/2, 6, ... form an A.P. with d = 3/2. 12th reciprocal = 3 + 11(3/2) = 39/2, so 12th term = 2/39.

mcqs.q: What is the first of the five harmonic means between 1/4 and 1/24?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals are 4 and 24, d = 20/6 = 10/3. First reciprocal mean = 4 + 10/3 = 22/3, so first H.M. = 3/22. Full set: 3/22, 3/32, 1/14, 3/52, 3/62.

mcqs.q: What are the four harmonic means between 1/3 and 1/23?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals are 3 and 23, d = 20/5 = 4, giving reciprocal means 7, 11, 15, 19. Hence H.Ms are 1/7, 1/11, 1/15, 1/19.

mcqs.q: The 7th and 10th terms of an H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21. What is its 14th term?
mcqs.why: Reciprocal A.P.: a + 6d = 3 and a + 9d = 21/5 give 3d = 6/5, d = 2/5, a = 3/5. 14th reciprocal = 3/5 + 13(2/5) = 29/5, so 14th term = 5/29.

mcqs.q: The first term of an H.P. is -1/3 and the fifth term is 1/5. What is its 9th term?
mcqs.why: Reciprocal A.P. has first term -3 and fifth term 5: -3 + 4d = 5 gives d = 2. 9th reciprocal = -3 + 8(2) = 13, so 9th term = 1/13.

mcqs.q: If 5 is the harmonic mean between 2 and b, what is b?
If 1/k, 1/(2k + 1) and 1/(4k - 1) are in harmonic sequence, what is k?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals k, 2k+1, 4k-1 must be in A.P.: 2(2k+1) = k + (4k-1) gives 4k+2 = 5k-1, so k = 3. The printed key reads 67, but the notes flag this: for k = 67, 2 x 135 = 270 is not 67 + 267 = 334, so the corrected value is k = 3.

mcqs.q: For the series 1 x 1 + 2 x 4 + 3 x 7 + ... with S_n = n(n + 1)(2n - 1)/2, what is S_2?
mcqs.why: Direct sum: 1x1 + 2x4 = 1 + 8 = 9. Check formula: S_2 = 2(3)(3)/2 = 9, since nth term is n(3n-2).

mcqs.q: For the series 1 x 3 + 3 x 6 + 5 x 9 + ... with S_n = n(n + 1)(4n - 1)/2, what is S_2?
mcqs.why: Direct sum: 1x3 + 3x6 = 3 + 18 = 21. Check formula: S_2 = 2(3)(7)/2 = 21, since nth term is (2n-1)(3n).

mcqs.q: For the series 1 x 4 + 2 x 7 + 3 x 10 + ... with S_n = n(n + 1)^2, what is S_2?
mcqs.why: Direct sum: 1x4 + 2x7 = 4 + 14 = 18. Check formula: S_2 = 2(3)^2 = 18, since nth term is n(3n+1).

mcqs.q: For the series 1^2 + 3^2 + 5^2 + ... with S_n = n(4n^2 - 1)/3, what is S_3?
mcqs.why: Direct sum: 1 + 9 + 25 = 35. Check formula: S_3 = 3(4(9)-1)/3 = 36 - 1 = 35, since nth term is (2n-1)^2.

mcqs.q: For the series 2 x 1^2 + 4 x 2^2 + 6 x 3^2 + ... with S_n = n^2(n + 1)^2/2, what is S_2?
mcqs.why: Direct sum: 2x1 + 4x4 = 2 + 16 = 18. Check formula: S_2 = (4 x 9)/2 = 18, since nth term is 2n^3.

mcqs.q: For the series 1 + (1 + 2) + (1 + 2 + 3) + ... with S_n = n(n + 1)(n + 2)/6, what is S_3?
mcqs.why: Direct sum: 1 + 3 + 6 = 10. Check formula: S_3 = 3(4)(5)/6 = 60/6 = 10, since nth term is n(n+1)/2.
Direct sum: 1 + (1+4) = 6. Check formula: S_2 = 2(9)(4)/12 = 72/12 = 6, since nth term is n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
Direct: 1 - 4 + 9 - 16 = -10. Formula from notes: sum = -n(2n+1) = -2(5) = -10, since each pair (2k-1)^2 - (2k)^2 = -(4k-1).

mcqs.q: A series has nth term 3n^2 + n + 1 and S_n = n(n^2 + 2n + 2). What is S_2?
A series has nth term 3n^2 + 2n + 1. Using the sum to 2n terms n(8n^2 + 10n + 5), what is the sum to 2 terms (n = 1)?
mcqs.why: Terms: k=1 gives 3+2+1 = 6; k=2 gives 12+4+1 = 17; sum to 2 terms = 23. Check formula with n = 1: 1 x (8 + 10 + 5) = 23.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 4! ?
mcqs.why: By definition 4! = 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24, multiplying all whole numbers from 4 down to 1.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 6! ?
mcqs.why: 6! = 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 720, multiplying the six factors in descending order.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 8! / 7! ?
mcqs.why: 8! / 7! = (8 x 7!) / 7! = 8, because the 7! in the numerator cancels the denominator completely.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 11! / (4! x 7!) ?
mcqs.why: 11!/(4!7!) = (11 x 10 x 9 x 8)/(4 x 3 x 2 x 1) = 7920/24 = 330 after cancelling 7! top and bottom.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 6! / (3! x 3!) ?
What is the value of 8! / (4! x 2!) ?
What is the value of 11! / (2! x 4! x 5!) ?
mcqs.why: 11! = 39916800 and 2! x 4! x 5! = 2 x 24 x 120 = 5760, so the value is 39916800/5760 = 6930. The printed key value 770 is wrong; the notes flag and correct it to 6930.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 9! / (2! x (9-2)!) ?
mcqs.why: 9!/(2!7!) = (9 x 8)/(2 x 1) = 72/2 = 36, after cancelling 7! from numerator and denominator.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 15! / (15! x (15-15)!) ?
20 x 19 x 18 x 17 written in factorial form is equal to which expression?
mcqs.why: 20!/16! = 20 x 19 x 18 x 17, because dividing 20! by 16! cancels all factors from 16 down to 1, leaving exactly those four factors.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.2
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-3

1. Evaluate the following: i) 20P3 ii) 16P4 iii) 12P5 iv) 10P7 v) 9P8 2. Find the value

of n when: i) nP2 = 30 ii) 11Pn = 11.10.9 iii) nP4 : (n-1)P3 = 9 : 1 3. Prove from the

first principle that: i) nPr = n . (n-1)P(r-1) ii) nPr = (n-1)Pr + r . (n-1)P(r-1)

1. i) 20P3 = 20 x 19 x 18 = 6840. ii) 16P4 = 16 x 15 x 14 x 13 = 43680. iii) 12P5 =

12 x 11 x 10 x 9 x 8 = 95040. iv) 10P7 = 10 x 9 x 8 x 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 = 604800. v) 9P8

= 9! = 362880.
2. i) nP2 = n(n-1) = 30, so n = 6 (since 6 x 5 = 30). ii) 11Pn = 11 x

10 x 9, so three factors are used and n = 3. iii) nP4/(n-1)P3 =

n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)/((n-1)(n-2)(n-3)) = n = 9/1, so n = 9.
3. i) By definition nPr =

n!/(n-r)! = n x (n-1)!/(n-r)! = n x (n-1)P(r-1), since (n-1)P(r-1) = (n-1)!/((n-1)-(r-1))! =

(n-1)!/(n-r)!. ii) (n-1)Pr + r x (n-1)P(r-1) = (n-1)!/(n-1-r)! + r(n-1)!/(n-r)! = (n-1)!/(n-r)!

x ((n-r) + r) = n(n-1)!/(n-r)! = n!/(n-r)! = nPr, as required.

Q4-7

4. How many signals can be given by 5 flags of different colours, using 3 flags at a

time? 5. How many signals can be given by 6 flags of different colours when any

number of flags can be used at a time? 6. How many words can be formed from the

letters of the following words using all letters when no letter is to be repeated: i)

PLANE ii) OBJECT iii) FASTING? 7. How many 3-digit numbers can be formed by using

each one of the digits 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 only once?

4.
The number of signals is 5P3 = 5 x 4 x 3 = 60. 5.
Using 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 flags at a

time: 6P1 + 6P2 + 6P3 + 6P4 + 6P5 + 6P6 = 6 + 30 + 120 + 360 + 720 + 720 =

1956 signals.
6. i) PLANE has 5 different letters: 5! = 120 words. ii) OBJECT has 6

different letters: 6! = 720 words. iii) FASTING has 7 different letters: 7! = 5040

words. 7.
The number of 3-digit numbers is 5P3 = 5 x 4 x 3 = 60.

Q8-11

8. Find the numbers greater than 23000 that can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3,

5, 6, without repeating any digit. HINT: The first two digits on L.H.S. will be 23 etc. 9.

Find the number of 5-digit numbers that can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 4, 6, 8

(when no digit is repeated), but i) the digits 2 and 8 are next to each other; ii) the

digits 2 and 8 are not next to each other. 10. How many 6-digit numbers can be

formed, without repeating any digit from the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5? In how many of

them will 0 be at the tens place? 11. How many 5-digit multiples of 5 can be formed

from the digits 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, when no digit is repeated.

8.
Only 5-digit numbers can exceed 23000.
First digit 3, 5 or 6: 3 x 4! = 72 numbers.

First digit 2: the second digit must be 3, 5 or 6 (a second digit 1 gives a number

below 23000), giving 3 x 3! = 18 numbers.
Total = 72 + 18 = 90. 9. All 5-digit

numbers: 5! = 120. i) Treating 2 and 8 as one block: 4! x 2 = 48 numbers. ii) Not

next to each other: 120 - 48 = 72 numbers. 10.
The first digit cannot be 0: 5 x 5! =

600 numbers.
With 0 fixed at the tens place, the first digit has 5 choices and the

remaining four places can be filled in 4! ways: 5 x 4! = 120 numbers. 11. A multiple

of 5 must end in 5, so the units place is fixed and the remaining four places can be

filled in 4! = 24 ways.

Q12-14

12. In how many ways can 8 books including 2 on English be arranged on a shelf in

such a way that the English books are never together? 13. Find the number of

arrangements of 3 books on English and 5 books on Urdu for placing them on a

shelf such that the books on the same subject are together. 14. In how many ways

can 5 boys and 4 girls be seated on a bench so that the girls and the boys occupy

alternate seats?

12.
All arrangements: 8! = 40320.
Arrangements with the two English books

together: treat them as one block, giving 7! x 2! = 10080.
Hence the English books

are never together in 40320 - 10080 = 30240 ways. 13.
The 3 English books can be

arranged in 3! ways and the 5 Urdu books in 5! ways, and the two subject-blocks

can be ordered in 2! ways: 2! x 3! x 5! = 2 x 6 x 120 = 1440 arrangements. 14.

With 9 seats alternating, the pattern must start and end with a boy: B G B G B G B G

B. The 5 boys can be seated in 5! ways and the 4 girls in 4! ways, giving 5! x 4! =

120 x 24 = 2880 ways.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 20P3 ?
mcqs.why: 20P3 = 20 x 19 x 18 = 6840, taking the product of the first 3 descending factors starting from 20.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 16P4 ?
mcqs.why: 16P4 = 16 x 15 x 14 x 13 = 43680, taking the product of 4 descending factors starting from 16.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 12P5 ?
mcqs.why: 12P5 = 12 x 11 x 10 x 9 x 8 = 95040, taking the product of 5 descending factors starting from 12.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 9P8 ?
mcqs.why: 9P8 = 9!/(9-8)! = 9!/1! = 362880, which is simply 9! since arranging 8 of 9 objects uses all but one factor.

mcqs.q: If nP2 = 30, what is the value of n ?
mcqs.why: nP2 = n(n-1) = 30. Trying n = 6 gives 6 x 5 = 30, so n = 6 satisfies the equation.

mcqs.q: If nP4 : (n-1)P3 = 9 : 1, what is the value of n ?
How many signals can be given by 5 flags of different colours, using 3 flags at a time?
mcqs.why: The order of the flags matters in a signal, so the number is 5P3 = 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 signals.

mcqs.q: How many signals can be given by 6 flags of different colours when any number of flags can be used at a time?
mcqs.why: Add all cases: 6P1+6P2+6P3+6P4+6P5+6P6 = 6+30+120+360+720+720 = 1956 signals in total.

mcqs.q: How many words can be formed from the letters of the word PLANE, using all letters with no letter repeated?
mcqs.why: PLANE has 5 different letters, so the words are the permutations of 5 letters: 5! = 120 words.

mcqs.q: How many numbers greater than 23000 can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 without repeating any digit?
mcqs.why: First digit 3, 5 or 6 gives 3 x 4! = 72 numbers. First digit 2 needs second digit 3, 5 or 6, giving 3 x 3! = 18 numbers. Total = 72 + 18 = 90.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.3
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-4

1. How many arrangements of the letters of the following words, taken all together,

can be made: i) PAKPATTAN ii) PAKISTAN iii) MATHEMATICS iv) ASSASSINATION? 2.

How many permutation of the letters of the word PANAMA can be made, if P is to be

the first letter in each arrangement? 3. How many arrangements of the letters of

the word ATTACKED can be made, if each arrangement begins with C and ends with

K? 4. How many numbers greater than 1000,000 can be formed from the digits 0, 2,

2, 2, 3, 4, 4?

1. i) PAKPATTAN has 9 letters with A 3 times, P 2 times and T 2 times: 9!/(3! 2! 2!) =

362880/24 = 15120. ii) PAKISTAN has 8 letters with A 2 times: 8!/2! = 20160. iii)

MATHEMATICS has 11 letters with M, A and T each 2 times: 11!/(2! 2! 2!) =

39916800/8 = 4989600. iv) ASSASSINATION has 13 letters with A 3 times, S 4

times, I 2 times and N 2 times: 13!/(3! 4! 2!
2!) = 6227020800/576 = 10810800. 2.

With P fixed first, the remaining letters A, N, A, M, A have A 3 times: 5!/3! = 20

arrangements. 3.
With C first and K last, the remaining letters A, T, T, A, E, D have A

2 times and T 2 times: 6!/(2!
2!) = 180 arrangements. 4.
All 7-digit numbers formed

from 0, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4 exceed 1000,000.
Total arrangements: 7!/(3! 2!) = 420.

Arrangements with first digit 0: 6!/(3! 2!) = 60.
Hence 420 - 60 = 360 numbers.

Q5-8

5. How many 6-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4? How

many of them will lie between 400,000 and 430,000? 6. 11 members of a club form

4 committees of 3, 4, 2, 2 members so that no member is a member of more than

one committee. Find the number of committees. 7. The D.C.Os of 11 districts meet

to discuss the law and order situation in their districts. In how many ways can they

be seated at a round table, when two particular D.C.Os insist on sitting together? 8.

The Governor of the Punjab calls a meeting of 12 officers.
In how many ways can

they be seated at a round table?

5.
Total 6-digit numbers: 6!/(2! 2! 2!) = 90.
Between 400,000 and 430,000 the first

digit must be 4 and the second digit must be 2 (a second digit 3 gives a number

above 430,000): the remaining digits 2, 3, 3, 4 can be arranged in 4!/2! = 12 ways.

Hence 12 numbers lie between 400,000 and 430,000. 6.
Choosing 3, then 4, then 2,

then 2 members: 11!/(3! 4! 2!
2!) = 39916800/576 = 69300 ways. NOTE: the key

gives 69300, i.e. the two committees of 2 are counted as distinct committees;

dividing by 2! for indistinguishable equal-size committees would give 34650. 7.

Treating the two particular D.C.Os as one block gives 10 objects at a round table:

(10-1)! = 9! = 362880, and the pair can sit in 2 orders, giving 2 x 362880 = 725760

ways. 8.
The printed key gives 19958400 = 11!/2 ways, i.e. the key counts a seating

and its mirror image as the same arrangement.
NOTE: counting rotations only, the

usual round-table count is (12-1)! = 11! = 39916800 ways.

Q9-12

9. Fatima invites 14 people to a dinner. There are 9 males and 5 females who are

seated at two different tables so that guests of one sex sit at one round table and

the guests of the other sex at the second table. Find the number of ways in which all

guests are seated. 10. Find the number of ways in which 5 men and 5 women can

be seated at a round table in such a way that no two persons of the same sex sit

together. 11. In how many ways can 4 keys be arranged on a circular key ring? 12.

How many necklaces can be made from 6 beads of different colours?

9.
The 9 males at one round table can be seated in (9-1)! = 8! = 40320 ways and

the 5 females at the other in (5-1)! = 4! = 24 ways, giving 40320 x 24 = 967680

ways. 10.
Fix one man to remove rotation: the remaining 4 men can be seated in 4!

ways in the alternate seats and the 5 women in 5! ways, giving 4! x 5! = 24 x 120 =

2880 ways. 11.
For a key ring, flipping gives the same arrangement, so the number

is (4-1)!/2 = 3 ways. 12.
For a necklace, flipping gives the same arrangement, so

the number is (6-1)!/2 = 60 necklaces.

mcqs.q: How many arrangements of the letters of the word PAKPATTAN, taken all together, can be made?
mcqs.why: PAKPATTAN has 9 letters with A 3 times, P 2 times and T 2 times: 9!/(3!2!2!) = 362880/24 = 15120 arrangements.

mcqs.q: How many arrangements of the letters of the word PAKISTAN, taken all together, can be made?
mcqs.why: PAKISTAN has 8 letters with A repeated 2 times: 8!/2! = 40320/2 = 20160 arrangements.

mcqs.q: How many arrangements of the letters of the word MATHEMATICS, taken all together, can be made?
mcqs.why: MATHEMATICS has 11 letters with M, A and T each 2 times: 11!/(2!2!2!) = 39916800/8 = 4989600 arrangements.

mcqs.q: How many arrangements of the letters of the word ASSASSINATION, taken all together, can be made?
mcqs.why: ASSASSINATION has 13 letters with A 3 times, S 4 times, I 2 times and N 2 times: 13!/(3!4!2!2!) = 6227020800/576 = 10810800.

mcqs.q: How many permutations of the letters of the word PANAMA can be made if P is the first letter in each arrangement?
mcqs.why: With P fixed first, the remaining letters A, N, A, M, A have A 3 times: 5!/3! = 120/6 = 20 arrangements.

mcqs.q: How many arrangements of the letters of the word ATTACKED begin with C and end with K?
mcqs.why: With C first and K last, the remaining letters A, T, T, A, E, D have A 2 times and T 2 times: 6!/(2!2!) = 720/4 = 180 arrangements.

mcqs.q: How many numbers greater than 1000,000 can be formed from the digits 0, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4?
mcqs.why: Total arrangements are 7!/(3!2!) = 420. Those with first digit 0 number 6!/(3!2!) = 60, and these are not 7-digit numbers, so 420 - 60 = 360 numbers remain.

mcqs.q: How many 6-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4?
mcqs.why: Each digit pair is repeated twice, so the count is 6!/(2!2!2!) = 720/8 = 90 numbers.

mcqs.q: How many of the 6-digit numbers formed from 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4 lie between 400,000 and 430,000?
mcqs.why: The first digit must be 4 and the second digit must be 2 (a second digit 3 exceeds 430,000). The remaining digits 2, 3, 3, 4 arrange in 4!/2! = 12 ways.

mcqs.q: 11 D.C.Os are seated at a round table and two particular D.C.Os insist on sitting together. In how many ways can they be seated?
mcqs.why: Treat the pair as one block, giving 10 objects at a round table: (10-1)! = 9! = 362880 seatings, and the pair has 2 internal orders, so 2 x 362880 = 725760 ways.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.4
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-3

1. Evaluate the following: i) 12C3 ii) 20C17 iii) nC4 2. Find the value of n, when i)

nC5 = nC4 ii) nC10 = (12 x 11)/(2!) iii) nC12 = nC6 3. Find the values of n and r,

when i) nCr = 35 and nPr = 210 ii) (n-1)C(r-1) : nCr : (n+1)C(r+1) = 3 : 6 : 11

1. i) 12C3 = (12 x 11 x 10)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 220. ii) 20C17 = 20C3 = (20 x 19 x 18)/6 =

1140. iii) nC4 = n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)/4!.
2. i) nC5 = nC4 gives 5 + 4 = n, so n = 9. ii)

nC10 = 66 = 12C10, so n = 12. iii) nC12 = nC6 gives 12 + 6 = n, so n = 18. 3. i)

nPr/nCr = r! = 210/35 = 6, so r = 3.
Then nC3 = 35 gives n(n-1)(n-2) = 210, so n =

7 (since 7 x 6 x 5 = 210). ii) nCr/(n-1)C(r-1) = n/r = 6/3 = 2, so n = 2r. Also

(n+1)C(r+1)/nCr = (n+1)/(r+1) = 11/6, so 6n + 6 = 11r + 11; with n = 2r this gives

12r + 6 = 11r + 11, so r = 5 and n = 10.

Q4-7

4. How many (a) diagonals and (b) triangles can be formed by joining the vertices of

the polygon having: i) 5 sides ii) 8 sides iii) 12 sides? 5. The members of a club are

12 boys and 8 girls. In how many ways can a committee of 3 boys and 2 girls be

formed? 6. How many committees of 5 members can be chosen from a group of 8

persons when each committee must include 2 particular persons? 7. In how many

ways can a hockey team of 11 players be selected out of 15 players? How many of

them will include a particular player?

4.
The number of diagonals of an n-sided polygon is nC2 - n and the number of

triangles is nC3. i) 5 sides: diagonals 10 - 5 = 5, triangles 10. ii) 8 sides: diagonals

28 - 8 = 20, triangles 56. iii) 12 sides: diagonals 66 - 12 = 54, triangles 220. NOTE:

the printed key lists one number per part (10, 20, 54); these are the pentagon

triangles, the octagon diagonals and the 12-gon diagonals respectively, all of which

appear above. 5.
12C3 x 8C2 = 220 x 28 = 6160 ways. 6.
With 2 particular persons

fixed, the remaining 3 members are chosen from the other 6 persons: 6C3 = 20

committees. 7.
15C11 = 1365 teams.
Teams including a particular player: choose

the remaining 10 from the other 14 players: 14C10 = 1001 teams.

Q8-10

8. Show that: 16C11 + 16C10 = 17C11 9. There are 8 men and 10 women members

of a club. How many committees of 7 can be formed, having: i) 4 women ii) at the

most 4 women iii) atleast 4 women? 10. Prove that nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr.

8.
By Pascal's rule, 16C11 + 16C10 = 17C11, since nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr with n

= 16 and r = 11. 9.
A committee of 7 with k women and 7-k men can be formed in

10Ck x 8C(7-k) ways. i) Exactly 4 women: 10C4 x 8C3 = 210 x 56 = 11760. ii) At

most 4 women: k = 0 to 4 gives 1 x 8 + 10 x 28 + 45 x 56 + 120 x 70 + 210 x 56 =

8 + 280 + 2520 + 8400 + 11760 = 22968. iii) At least 4 women: k = 4 to 7 gives

11760 + 252 x 28 + 210 x 8 + 120 x 1 = 11760 + 7056 + 1680 + 120 = 20616.

NOTE: the committee size 7 is the value forced by the printed key (all three key

values 11760, 22968, 20616 are reproduced exactly by committees of 7). 10. nCr +

nC(r-1) = n!/(r!(n-r)!) + n!/((r-1)!(n-r+1)!) = n!/((r-1)!(n-r)!) x (1/r + 1/(n-r+1)) =

n!/((r-1)!(n-r)!) x (n+1)/(r(n-r+1)) = (n+1)!/(r!(n+1-r)!) = (n+1)Cr, as required.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 12C3 ?
mcqs.why: 12C3 = (12 x 11 x 10)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 1320/6 = 220, dividing the product of 3 descending factors by 3!.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 20C17 ?
If nC5 = nC4, what is the value of n ?
mcqs.why: When nCa = nCb with a not equal to b, then a + b = n. Here 5 + 4 = 9, so n = 9.

mcqs.q: If nC12 = nC6, what is the value of n ?
mcqs.why: When nCa = nCb with a not equal to b, then a + b = n. Here 12 + 6 = 18, so n = 18.

mcqs.q: If nCr = 35 and nPr = 210, what is the value of n ?
mcqs.why: nPr/nCr = r! = 210/35 = 6, so r = 3. Then nC3 = 35 gives n(n-1)(n-2) = 210 = 7 x 6 x 5, so n = 7.

mcqs.q: How many diagonals can be formed by joining the vertices of a polygon having 8 sides?
mcqs.why: Diagonals = nC2 - n = 8C2 - 8 = 28 - 8 = 20, subtracting the 8 sides themselves from all joins of vertex pairs.

mcqs.q: How many triangles can be formed by joining the vertices of a polygon having 12 sides?
mcqs.why: Triangles = nC3 = 12C3 = (12 x 11 x 10)/6 = 1320/6 = 220, choosing any 3 vertices of the 12.

mcqs.q: A club has 12 boys and 8 girls. In how many ways can a committee of 3 boys and 2 girls be formed?
mcqs.why: Choose the boys and girls independently and multiply: 12C3 x 8C2 = 220 x 28 = 6160 ways.

mcqs.q: How many committees of 5 members can be chosen from a group of 8 persons when each committee must include 2 particular persons?
mcqs.why: The 2 particular persons are already in, so choose the remaining 3 members from the other 6 persons: 6C3 = 20 committees.

mcqs.q: In how many ways can a hockey team of 11 players be selected out of 15 players?
mcqs.why: The team is a selection, so the count is 15C11 = 15C4 = (15 x 14 x 13 x 12)/24 = 32760/24 = 1365 teams.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.5
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-4

For the following experiments, find the probability in each case: 1. Experiment: From

a box containing orange-flavoured sweets, Bilal takes out one sweet without

looking. Events Happening: i) the sweet is orange-flavoured ii) the sweet is

lemon-flavoured. 2. Experiment: Pakistan and India play a cricket match. The result

is: Events Happening: i) Pakistan wins ii) India does not lose. 3. Experiment: There

are 5 green and 3 red balls in a box, one ball is taken out. Events Happening: i) the

ball is green ii) the ball is red. 4. Experiment: A fair coin is tossed three times. It

shows Events Happening: i) One tail ii) atleast one head.

1.
The box contains only orange-flavoured sweets. i) P(orange) = 1. ii) P(lemon) = 0.

2.
The three equally likely results are: Pakistan wins, India wins, draw. i) P(Pakistan

wins) = 1/3. ii) India does not lose means India wins or the match is drawn: P = 2/3.

3.
There are 8 balls in all. i) P(green) = 5/8. ii) P(red) = 3/8. 4.
The sample space has

2^3 = 8 equally likely outcomes. i) Exactly one tail occurs in HTT, THT, TTH: P =

3/8. ii) At least one head occurs in all outcomes except TTT: P = 7/8.

Q5-6

5. Experiment: A die is rolled. The top shows Events Happening: i) 3 or 4 dots ii)

dots less than 5. 6. Experiment: From a box containing slips numbered 1, 2, 3, ..., 5

one slip is picked up. Events Happening: i) the number on the slip is a prime number

ii) the number on the slip is a multiple of 3. 7.
Experiment: Two dice, one red and

the other blue, are rolled simultaneously.
The numbers of dots on the tops are

added.
The total of the two scores is: Events Happening: i) 5 ii) 7 iii) 11

5.
The sample space has 6 outcomes. i) P(3 or 4) = 2/6 = 1/3. ii) Dots less than 5

are 1, 2, 3, 4: P = 4/6 = 2/3. 6.
The sample space has 5 slips. i) Prime numbers

among 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are 2, 3, 5: P = 3/5. ii) The only multiple of 3 is 3: P = 1/5. 7. The

sample space has 36 outcomes. i) Sum 5 occurs as (1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1): P = 4/36

= 1/9. ii) Sum 7 occurs as (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): P = 6/36 = 1/6. iii)

Sum 11 occurs as (5,6), (6,5): P = 2/36 = 1/18.

8.
Experiment: A bag contains 40 balls out of which 5 are green, 15 are black and

the remaining are yellow.
A ball is taken out of the bag.
Events Happening: i) The

ball is black ii) The ball is green iii) The ball is not green. 9.
Experiment: One chit out

of 30 containing the names of 30 students of a class of 18 boys and 12 girls is taken

out at random, for nomination as the monitor of the class.
Events Happening: i) the

monitor is a boy ii) the monitor is a girl. 10.
Experiment: A coin is tossed four times.

The tops show Events Happening: i) all heads ii) 2 heads and 2 tails.

8.
The remaining balls are 40 - 5 - 15 = 20 yellow balls. i) P(black) = 15/40 = 3/8. ii)

P(green) = 5/40 = 1/8. iii) P(not green) = 35/40 = 7/8. 9.
There are 30 chits. i)

P(boy) = 18/30 = 3/5. ii) P(girl) = 12/30 = 2/5. 10.
The sample space has 2^4 = 16

outcomes. i) All heads occurs only as HHHH: P = 1/16. ii) 2 heads and 2 tails occurs

in 4C2 = 6 outcomes: P = 6/16 = 3/8.
NOTE: the printed Answers block for Exercise

7.5 lists values for Q1-Q7 only; the values for Q8-Q10 above are computed directly

from the experiments.

mcqs.q: A box contains only orange-flavoured sweets and Bilal takes out one sweet without looking. What is the probability that the sweet is orange-flavoured?
mcqs.why: Every sweet in the box is orange-flavoured, so the event is certain: favourable outcomes equal all outcomes, giving probability 1.

mcqs.q: From the same box containing only orange-flavoured sweets, what is the probability that a sweet taken out is lemon-flavoured?
mcqs.why: There are no lemon-flavoured sweets in the box at all, so the event is impossible and its probability is 0.

mcqs.q: Pakistan and India play a cricket match with three equally likely results: Pakistan wins, India wins, or a draw. What is the probability that Pakistan wins?
mcqs.why: There is 1 favourable result (Pakistan wins) out of 3 equally likely results, so the probability is 1/3.

mcqs.q: In the same cricket match, what is the probability that India does not lose?
mcqs.why: India does not lose means India wins or the match is drawn: 2 favourable results out of 3 equally likely results, giving 2/3.

mcqs.q: There are 5 green and 3 red balls in a box and one ball is taken out. What is the probability that the ball is green?
mcqs.why: There are 5 + 3 = 8 balls in all, of which 5 are green, so P(green) = 5/8.

mcqs.q: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of getting exactly one tail?
mcqs.why: The sample space has 2^3 = 8 outcomes. Exactly one tail occurs in HTT, THT and TTH, which is 3 outcomes, so the probability is 3/8.

mcqs.q: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
mcqs.why: The only outcome with no head is TTT, 1 of the 8 outcomes. So P(at least one head) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.

mcqs.q: A die is rolled. What is the probability that the top shows 3 or 4 dots?
mcqs.why: The favourable outcomes are 3 and 4, which is 2 outcomes out of 6, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

mcqs.q: A slip is picked from slips numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. What is the probability that the number on the slip is a prime number?
mcqs.why: The prime numbers among 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are 2, 3 and 5, which is 3 favourable slips out of 5, giving 3/5.

mcqs.q: Two dice, one red and the other blue, are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability that the total is 7?
mcqs.why: A total of 7 occurs as (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): 6 outcomes out of 36, so the probability is 6/36 = 1/6.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.6
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-2

1. A fair coin is tossed 30 times, the result of which is tabulated below. Study the

table and answer the questions given below the table: Event: Head, Tally Marks: 14;

Event: Tail, Tally Marks: 16. i) How many times does 'head' appear? ii) How many

times does 'tail' appear? iii) Estimate the probability of the appearance of head? iv)

Estimate the probability of the appearance of tail? 2. A die is tossed 100 times. The

result is tabulated below. Study the table and answer the questions given below the

table: Frequencies: 1: 14, 2: 17, 3: 20, 4: 18, 5: 15, 6: 16. i) How many times do 3

dots appear? ii) How many times do 5 dots appear? iii) How many times does an

even number of dots appear? iv) How many times does a prime number of dots

appear? v) Find the probability of each one of the above cases.

1. i) Head appears 14 times. ii) Tail appears 16 times. iii) The estimated probability

of head is 14/30 = 7/15. iv) The estimated probability of tail is 16/30 = 8/15. 2. i) 3

dots appear 20 times. ii) 5 dots appear 15 times. iii) An even number of dots (2, 4,

6) appears 17 + 18 + 16 = 51 times. iv) A prime number of dots (2, 3, 5) appears

17 + 20 + 15 = 52 times. v) The estimated probabilities are: 20/100 = 1/5 for 3

dots; 15/100 = 3/20 for 5 dots; 51/100 for an even number; 52/100 = 13/25 for a

prime number.

Q3

3. The eggs supplied by a poultry farm during a week broke during transit as

follows: 1 %, 2 %, 1 1/2 %, 1/2 %, 1 %, 2 %, 1 %. Find the probability of the eggs

that broke in a day. Calculate the number of eggs that will be broken in transiting

the following number of eggs: i) 7,000 ii) 8,400 iii) 10,500

3.
The total breakage over the 7 days is 1 + 2 + 1.5 + 0.5 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 9 %.

Hence the probability that an egg breaks in a day is 9/(7 x 100) = 9/700. i) Out of

7,000 eggs: 7000 x 9/700 = 90 eggs. ii) Out of 8,400 eggs: 8400 x 9/700 = 108

eggs. iii) Out of 10,500 eggs: 10500 x 9/700 = 135 eggs.

mcqs.q: A fair coin is tossed 30 times and the tally for head is 14. How many times does head appear?
mcqs.why: The tally marks recorded for the event Head in the table are 14, so head appears 14 times in the 30 tosses.

mcqs.q: In the same experiment of 30 coin tosses, the tally for tail is 16. How many times does tail appear?
mcqs.why: The tally marks recorded for the event Tail in the table are 16, so tail appears 16 times, and 14 + 16 = 30 tosses in all.

mcqs.q: Using the 30 coin tosses (head 14 times), what is the estimated probability of the appearance of head?
mcqs.why: Estimated probability = frequency / total trials = 14/30 = 7/15 after dividing numerator and denominator by 2.

mcqs.q: Using the 30 coin tosses (tail 16 times), what is the estimated probability of the appearance of tail?
mcqs.why: Estimated probability = frequency / total trials = 16/30 = 8/15 after dividing numerator and denominator by 2.

mcqs.q: A die is tossed 100 times with frequencies 1:14, 2:17, 3:20, 4:18, 5:15, 6:16. How many times do 3 dots appear?
mcqs.why: The frequency table gives the frequency of the face with 3 dots directly as 20 out of the 100 tosses.

mcqs.q: Using the same 100 die tosses, how many times does an even number of dots appear?
mcqs.why: The even faces are 2, 4 and 6 with frequencies 17, 18 and 16. Adding them: 17 + 18 + 16 = 51 times.

mcqs.q: Using the same 100 die tosses, how many times does a prime number of dots appear?
mcqs.why: The prime faces are 2, 3 and 5 with frequencies 17, 20 and 15. Adding them: 17 + 20 + 15 = 52 times.

mcqs.q: Using the same 100 die tosses, what is the estimated probability of getting 5 dots?
mcqs.why: The frequency of 5 dots is 15, so the estimated probability is 15/100 = 3/20 after dividing by 5.

mcqs.q: Using the same 100 die tosses, what is the estimated probability of getting an even number of dots?
mcqs.why: An even number appears 17 + 18 + 16 = 51 times out of 100 tosses, so the estimated probability is 51/100.

mcqs.q: Eggs broke in transit during a week at rates 1%, 2%, 1.5%, 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 1%. How many eggs are expected to break when 8,400 eggs are transported?
mcqs.why: Total breakage over 7 days is 1+2+1.5+0.5+1+2+1 = 9 percent, so the breakage probability is 9/(7 x 100) = 9/700. Expected broken eggs = 8400 x 9/700 = 108.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.7
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-4

1. If sample space S = {1, 2, 3, ..., 9}, Event A = {2, 4, 6, 8} and Event B = {1, 3,

5}, find P(A union B). 2. A box contains 10 red, 30 white and 20 black marbles. A

marble is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is either red or white. 3. A

natural number is chosen out of the first fifty natural numbers. What is the

probability that the chosen number is a multiple of 3 or of 5? 4. A card is drawn from

a deck of 52 playing cards. What is the probability that it is a diamond card or an

ace?

1.
A and B are disjoint, so P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) = 4/9 + 3/9 = 7/9. 2. The box

has 60 marbles; red or white marbles number 10 + 30 = 40, so P = 40/60 = 2/3. 3.

Multiples of 3 among the first 50 numbers: 16; multiples of 5: 10; multiples of both

(i.e. of 15): 3.
Hence multiples of 3 or 5 number 16 + 10 - 3 = 23, so P = 23/50. 4.

P(diamond) = 13/52, P(ace) = 4/52, P(diamond and ace) = 1/52, so P = 13/52 +

4/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.

Q5-7

5. A die is thrown twice. What is the probability that the sum of the number of dots

shown is 3 or 11? 6. Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the

number of dots appearing on them is 4 or 6? 7. Two dice are thrown simultaneously.

If the event A is that the sum of the number of dots shown is an odd number and

the event B is that the number of dots shown on at least one die is 3. Find P(A union

Q8

B). 8. There are 10 girls and 20 boys in a class. Half of the boys and half of the girls

have blue eyes. Find the probability that one student chosen as monitor is either a

girl or has blue eyes.

5.
Sum 3 occurs in 2 ways and sum 11 in 2 ways, out of 36 outcomes: P = 4/36 =

1/9. 6.
Sum 4 occurs in 3 ways and sum 6 in 5 ways: P = 8/36 = 2/9. 7. P(A) = 18/36

(half of all outcomes have odd sum).
P(B) = 11/36 (outcomes with at least one 3). A

and B together: outcomes with a 3 and odd sum are (3,2), (3,4), (3,6), (2,3), (4,3),

(6,3): 6 outcomes, so P(A and B) = 6/36.
Hence P(A union B) = 18/36 + 11/36 - 6/36

= 23/36. 8.
The class has 30 students.
Girls: 10; students with blue eyes: half of 20

boys (10) plus half of 10 girls (5) = 15; girls with blue eyes: 5.
Hence P(girl or blue

eyes) = 10/30 + 15/30 - 5/30 = 20/30 = 2/3.

mcqs.q: Sample space S = {1, 2, ..., 9}, A = {2, 4, 6, 8} and B = {1, 3, 5}. What is P(A union B)?
mcqs.why: A and B are disjoint, so P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) = 4/9 + 3/9 = 7/9, with no overlap term to subtract.

mcqs.q: A box contains 10 red, 30 white and 20 black marbles. A marble is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is either red or white?
mcqs.why: The box has 60 marbles in all and red or white marbles number 10 + 30 = 40, so the probability is 40/60 = 2/3.

mcqs.q: A natural number is chosen out of the first fifty natural numbers. What is the probability that it is a multiple of 3 or of 5?
mcqs.why: Multiples of 3 number 16, multiples of 5 number 10, and multiples of both (of 15) number 3. So multiples of 3 or 5 number 16 + 10 - 3 = 23, giving 23/50.

mcqs.q: A card is drawn from a deck of 52 playing cards. What is the probability that it is a diamond card or an ace?
mcqs.why: P(diamond) + P(ace) - P(ace of diamonds) = 13/52 + 4/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13, subtracting the ace of diamonds counted twice.

mcqs.q: A die is thrown twice. What is the probability that the sum of the dots shown is 3 or 11?
mcqs.why: Sum 3 occurs in 2 ways and sum 11 occurs in 2 ways out of 36 outcomes, so the probability is 4/36 = 1/9.

mcqs.q: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the dots appearing is 4 or 6?
mcqs.why: Sum 4 occurs in 3 ways and sum 6 occurs in 5 ways out of 36 outcomes, so the probability is 8/36 = 2/9.

mcqs.q: Two dice are thrown. A is the event that the sum is odd and B is the event that at least one die shows 3. What is P(A union B)?
mcqs.why: P(A) = 18/36, P(B) = 11/36, and A and B together occur in 6 outcomes, so P(A union B) = 18/36 + 11/36 - 6/36 = 23/36.

mcqs.q: There are 10 girls and 20 boys in a class. Half of the boys and half of the girls have blue eyes. What is the probability that a student chosen as monitor is either a girl or has blue eyes?
mcqs.why: Girls number 10, students with blue eyes number 10 + 5 = 15, and girls with blue eyes number 5. So the probability is 10/30 + 15/30 - 5/30 = 20/30 = 2/3.

mcqs.q: How many numbers among the first fifty natural numbers are multiples of 3 or of 5?
mcqs.why: Multiples of 3 number 16 and multiples of 5 number 10, but multiples of 15 (3 numbers) are counted in both, so the count is 16 + 10 - 3 = 23.

mcqs.q: Two dice are thrown. B is the event that the number of dots shown on at least one die is 3. What is P(B)?
mcqs.why: Outcomes with at least one 3 are the 6 outcomes with first die 3 plus the 5 further outcomes with second die 3, giving 11 outcomes out of 36, so P(B) = 11/36.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.8
lessons.notes_html:
Q1-5

1. The probability that a person A will be alive 15 year hence is 5/7 and the

probability that another person B will be alive 15 years hence is 7/9. Find the

probability that both will be alive 15 year hence. 2. A die is rolled twice: Event E1 is

the appearance of even number of dots and event E2 is the appearance of more

than 4 dots. Prove that: P(E1 and E2) = P(E1).P(E2). 3. Determine the probability of

getting 2 heads in two successive tosses of a balanced coin. 4. Two coins are tossed

twice each. Find the probability that the head appears on the first toss and the

same faces appear in the two tosses. 5. Two cards are drawn from a deck of 52

playing cards. If one card is drawn and replaced before drawing the second card,

find the probability that both the cards are aces.

1.
The two lives are independent, so P(both alive) = (5/7) x (7/9) = 5/9. 2. For one

roll, P(E1) = 3/6 = 1/2 (even dots 2, 4, 6) and P(E2) = 2/6 = 1/3 (dots more than 4

are 5, 6).
The event E1 and E2 together is the dot 6: P = 1/6 = (1/2) x (1/3) = P(E1)

x P(E2), as required. 3.
P(2 heads) = (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4. 4.
P(head on the first toss)

= 1/2.
P(the same face in the two tosses) = P(HH or TT) = 1/2. The tosses are

independent, so P = (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4. 5.
With replacement, P(both aces) = (4/52)

x (4/52) = 1/169.

Q6-10

6. Two cards from a deck of 52 playing cards are drawn in such a way that the card

is replaced after the first draw. Find the probabilities in the following cases: i) first

card is king and the second is a queen. ii) both the cards are faced cards i.e. king,

queen, jack. 7. Two dice are thrown twice. What is probability that sum of the dots

shown in the first throw is 7 and that of the second throw is 11? 8. Find the

probability that the sum of dots appearing in two successive throws of two dice is

every time 7. 9. A fair die is thrown twice. Find the probability that a prime number

of dots appear in the first throw and the number of dots in the second throw is less

than 5. 10. A bag contains 8 red, 5 white and 7 black balls. 3 balls are drawn from

the bag. What is the probability that the first ball is red, the second ball is white and

the third ball is black, when every time the ball is replaced? HINT: (8/20)(5/20)(7/20)

is the probability.

6. i) P(king then queen) = (4/52) x (4/52) = 1/169. ii) There are 12 face cards, so

P(both face cards) = (12/52) x (12/52) = 9/169.
FLAG: the printed key reads 3/169

for this part, but (12/52) x (12/52) = 144/2704 = 9/169. 7.
P(sum 7 in the first

throw) = 6/36 = 1/6 and P(sum 11 in the second throw) = 2/36 = 1/18; the throws

are independent, so P = (1/6) x (1/18) = 1/108. 8.
P(sum 7 in one throw) = 6/36 =

1/6, so P(sum 7 in both throws) = (1/6) x (1/6) = 1/36. 9.
P(prime in the first throw)

= 3/6 = 1/2 (primes 2, 3, 5) and P(less than 5 in the second throw) = 4/6 = 2/3, so P

= (1/2) x (2/3) = 1/3. 10.
With replacement, P = (8/20) x (5/20) x (7/20) = 280/8000

= 7/200.

mcqs.q: The probability that A will be alive 15 years hence is 5/7 and that B will be alive is 7/9. What is the probability that both will be alive?
mcqs.why: The two lives are independent, so P(both alive) = (5/7) x (7/9) = 35/63 = 5/9 after cancelling the factor 7.

mcqs.q: What is the probability of getting 2 heads in two successive tosses of a balanced coin?
mcqs.why: The tosses are independent, so P(2 heads) = (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4, multiplying the probability of a head on each toss.

mcqs.q: Two cards are drawn from a deck of 52 cards, the first card being replaced before the second draw. What is the probability that both cards are aces?
mcqs.why: With replacement the draws are independent: P(both aces) = (4/52) x (4/52) = (1/13) x (1/13) = 1/169.

mcqs.q: Two cards are drawn with replacement from a deck of 52 cards. What is the probability that both cards are face cards (king, queen or jack)?
mcqs.why: There are 12 face cards, so P = (12/52) x (12/52) = 144/2704 = 9/169. The printed key value 3/169 is wrong; the notes flag and correct it to 9/169.

mcqs.q: Two dice are thrown twice. What is the probability that the sum in the first throw is 7 and the sum in the second throw is 11?
mcqs.why: P(sum 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 and P(sum 11) = 2/36 = 1/18. The throws are independent, so P = (1/6) x (1/18) = 1/108.

mcqs.q: What is the probability that the sum of dots in two successive throws of two dice is 7 every time?
mcqs.why: P(sum 7 in one throw) = 6/36 = 1/6. For both throws, by independence, P = (1/6) x (1/6) = 1/36.

mcqs.q: A fair die is thrown twice. What is the probability that a prime number appears in the first throw and a number less than 5 appears in the second throw?
mcqs.why: P(prime) = 3/6 = 1/2 for primes 2, 3, 5, and P(less than 5) = 4/6 = 2/3. By independence, P = (1/2) x (2/3) = 1/3.

mcqs.q: A bag contains 8 red, 5 white and 7 black balls. Three balls are drawn one by one with replacement. What is the probability that the first is red, the second white and the third black?
mcqs.why: With replacement each draw is from 20 balls: P = (8/20) x (5/20) x (7/20) = 280/8000 = 7/200 after simplifying.

mcqs.q: For one roll of a die, E1 is an even number of dots and E2 is more than 4 dots. What is P(E1 and E2)?
mcqs.why: P(E1) = 3/6 = 1/2 and P(E2) = 2/6 = 1/3. The event E1 and E2 together is only the dot 6, so P = 1/6 = (1/2) x (1/3), confirming independence.

mcqs.q: In two successive tosses of a coin, what is the probability that the same faces appear in the two tosses?
mcqs.why: The same face means HH or TT. P(HH or TT) = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, since each of HH and TT has probability (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Mathematical Induction and Binomial Theorem

lessons.title: Exercise 8.1
lessons.notes_html:
Q1

Use mathematical induction to prove for every positive integer n: 1. 1 + 5 + 9 + ...

+ (4n - 3) = n(2n - 1)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = 1 x (2 - 1) = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 1 + 5

+ ... + (4k - 3) = k(2k - 1).
Adding the next term (4(k + 1) - 3) = 4k + 1 to both

sides gives k(2k - 1) + 4k + 1 = 2k^2 + 3k + 1 = (k + 1)(2k + 1) = (k + 1)(2(k + 1)

- 1), which is the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q2

2. 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1) = n^2

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 1 + 3

+ ... + (2k - 1) = k^2.
Adding the next term (2(k + 1) - 1) = 2k + 1 gives k^2 + 2k

+ 1 = (k + 1)^2, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q3

3. 1 + 4 + 7 + ... + (3n - 2) = n(3n - 1)/2

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = 1 x 2/2 = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 1 + 4

+ ... + (3k - 2) = k(3k - 1)/2.
Adding the next term (3(k + 1) - 2) = 3k + 1 gives k(3k

- 1)/2 + 3k + 1 = (3k^2 - k + 6k + 2)/2 = (3k^2 + 5k + 2)/2 = (k + 1)(3k + 2)/2 =

(k + 1)(3(k + 1) - 1)/2, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q4

4. 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(n-1) = 2^n - 1

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = 2 - 1 = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 1 + 2

+ ... + 2^(k-1) = 2^k - 1.
Adding the next term 2^k gives 2^k - 1 + 2^k =

2^(k+1) - 1, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q5

5. 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... + 1/2^(n-1) = 2[1 - 1/2^n]

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = 2(1 - 1/2) = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 1 + 1/2

+ ... + 1/2^(k-1) = 2(1 - 1/2^k).
Adding the next term 1/2^k gives 2 - 2/2^k +

1/2^k = 2 - 1/2^k = 2(1 - 1/2^(k+1)), the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q6

6. 2 + 4 + 6 + ... + 2n = n(n + 1)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 2, RHS = 1 x 2 = 2. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 2 + 4

+ ... + 2k = k(k + 1).
Adding the next term 2(k + 1) gives k(k + 1) + 2(k + 1) = (k

+ 1)(k + 2), the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q7

7. 2 + 6 + 18 + ... + 2 x 3^(n-1) = 3^n - 1

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 2, RHS = 3 - 1 = 2. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 2 + 6

+ ... + 2 x 3^(k-1) = 3^k - 1.
Adding the next term 2 x 3^k gives 3^k - 1 + 2 x 3^k

= 3^(k+1) - 1, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q8

8. 1x3 + 2x5 + 3x7 + ... + n x (2n + 1) = n(n + 1)(4n + 5)/6

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 3, RHS = 1 x 2 x 9/6 = 3. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is k(k + 1)(4k + 5)/6.
Adding the next term (k + 1)(2k + 3) gives (k +

1)[k(4k + 5)/6 + 2k + 3] = (k + 1)(4k^2 + 5k + 12k + 18)/6 = (k + 1)(4k^2 + 17k

+ 18)/6 = (k + 1)(k + 2)(4k + 9)/6 = (k + 1)(k + 2)(4(k + 1) + 5)/6, the statement

for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q9

9. 1x2 + 2x3 + 3x4 + ... + n x (n + 1) = n(n + 1)(n + 2)/3

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 2, RHS = 1 x 2 x 3/3 = 2. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is k(k + 1)(k + 2)/3.
Adding the next term (k + 1)(k + 2) gives (k + 1)(k

+ 2)(k/3 + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)(k + 3)/3, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q10

10. 1x2 + 3x4 + 5x6 + ... + (2n - 1) x 2n = n(n + 1)(4n - 1)/3

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 2, RHS = 1 x 2 x 3/3 = 2. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is k(k + 1)(4k - 1)/3.
Adding the next term (2k + 1)(2k + 2) = 2(k +

1)(2k + 1) gives (k + 1)[k(4k - 1)/3 + 2(2k + 1)] = (k + 1)(4k^2 - k + 12k + 6)/3 =

(k + 1)(4k^2 + 11k + 6)/3 = (k + 1)(k + 2)(4k + 3)/3 = (k + 1)(k + 2)(4(k + 1) -

1)/3, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q11

11. 1/(1x2) + 1/(2x3) + 1/(3x4) + ... + 1/(n(n + 1)) = 1 - 1/(n + 1)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1/2, RHS = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is 1 - 1/(k + 1) = k/(k + 1).
Adding the next term 1/((k + 1)(k + 2))

gives k/(k + 1) + 1/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = (k(k + 2) + 1)/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = (k + 1)^2/((k

+ 1)(k + 2)) = (k + 1)/(k + 2) = 1 - 1/(k + 2), the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q12

12. 1/(1x3) + 1/(3x5) + 1/(5x7) + ... + 1/((2n - 1)(2n + 1)) = n/(2n + 1)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1/3, RHS = 1/3. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is k/(2k + 1).
Adding the next term gives k/(2k + 1) + 1/((2k + 1)(2k +

3)) = (k(2k + 3) + 1)/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)) = (2k^2 + 3k + 1)/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)) = (k +

1)(2k + 1)/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)) = (k + 1)/(2k + 3) = (k + 1)/(2(k + 1) + 1), the

statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q13

13. 1/(2x5) + 1/(5x8) + 1/(8x11) + ... + 1/((3n - 1)(3n + 2)) = n/(2(3n + 2))

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1/10, RHS = 1/(2 x 5) = 1/10. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is k/(2(3k + 2)).
Note 1/((3k + 2)(3k + 5)) = (1/3)(1/(3k + 2) - 1/(3k +

5)).
Adding the next term: k/(2(3k + 2)) + 1/((3k + 2)(3k + 5)) = (k(3k + 5) +

2)/(2(3k + 2)(3k + 5)) = (3k^2 + 5k + 2)/(2(3k + 2)(3k + 5)) = (k + 1)(3k +

2)/(2(3k + 2)(3k + 5)) = (k + 1)/(2(3k + 5)) = (k + 1)/(2(3(k + 1) + 2)), the

statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q14

14. r + r^2 + r^3 + ... + r^n = r(1 - r^n)/(1 - r), (r != 1)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = r, RHS = r(1 - r)/(1 - r) = r. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume r + ...

+ r^k = r(1 - r^k)/(1 - r).
Adding the next term r^(k+1) gives r(1 - r^k)/(1 - r) +

r^(k+1) = r[(1 - r^k) + r^k(1 - r)]/(1 - r) = r(1 - r^(k+1))/(1 - r), the statement for n

= k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q15

15. a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + ... + [a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d]

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = a, RHS = (1/2)(2a) = a. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is k/2 [2a + (k - 1)d].
Adding the next term a + kd gives k/2 [2a + (k -

1)d] + a + kd = (2ak + k(k - 1)d + 2a + 2kd)/2 = ((k + 1)(2a) + k(k + 1)d)/2 = (k +

1)/2 [2a + kd], the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q16

16. 1 x |1 + 2 x |2 + 3 x |3 + ... + n x |n = |n+1 - 1 (here |n means n!)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1 x 1 = 1, RHS = 2! - 1 = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 1 x 1!

+ ... + k x k! = (k + 1)! - 1.
Adding the next term (k + 1) x (k + 1)! gives (k + 1)! - 1

+ (k + 1)(k + 1)! = (k + 2)(k + 1)! - 1 = (k + 2)! - 1, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q17

17. a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d when a_1, a_1 + d, a_1 + 2d, ... form an A.P.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: a_1 = a_1 + 0 x d. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume a_k =

a_1 + (k - 1)d.
The next term of the A.P. is a_(k+1) = a_k + d = a_1 + (k - 1)d + d =

a_1 + kd, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q18

18. a_n = a_1 r^(n-1) when a_1, a_1 r, a_1 r^2, ... form a G.P.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: a_1 = a_1 r^0. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume a_k =

a_1 r^(k-1).
The next term of the G.P. is a_(k+1) = a_k x r = a_1 r^(k-1) x r = a_1

r^k, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q19

19. 1^2 + 3^2 + 5^2 + ... + (2n - 1)^2 = n(4n^2 - 1)/3

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = 1 x 3/3 = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is k(4k^2 - 1)/3.
Adding the next term (2k + 1)^2 gives k(4k^2 - 1)/3 +

(2k + 1)^2 = (4k^3 - k + 3(4k^2 + 4k + 1))/3 = (4k^3 + 12k^2 + 11k + 3)/3 = (k

+ 1)(4k^2 + 8k + 3)/3 = (k + 1)(4(k + 1)^2 - 1)/3, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q20

20. C(3,3) + C(4,3) + C(5,3) + ... + C(n + 2,3) = C(n + 3,4) (hockey-stick identity)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = C(3,3) = 1, RHS = C(4,4) = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume C(3,3)

+ ... + C(k + 2,3) = C(k + 3,4).
Adding the next term C(k + 3,3) and using Pascal's

identity C(m,4) + C(m,3) = C(m + 1,4) with m = k + 3 gives C(k + 3,4) + C(k + 3,3)

= C(k + 4,4), the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q21

21. Prove by mathematical induction that for all positive integral values of n: i) n^2

+ n is divisible by 2. ii) 5^n - 2^n is divisible by 3. iii) 5^n - 1 is divisible by 4. iv) 8

x 10^n - 2 is divisible by 6. v) n^3 - n is divisible by 6.

(i) Step 1: For n = 1: 1 + 1 = 2, divisible by 2.
Step 2: Assume k^2 + k = 2m. Then

(k + 1)^2 + (k + 1) = k^2 + 3k + 2 = (k^2 + k) + 2(k + 1) = 2m + 2(k + 1),

divisible by 2.
(ii) Step 1: For n = 1: 5 - 2 = 3, divisible by 3.
Step 2: Assume 5^k -

2^k = 3m.
Then 5^(k+1) - 2^(k+1) = 5(5^k - 2^k) + 3 x 2^k = 15m + 3 x 2^k,

divisible by 3.
(iii) Step 1: For n = 1: 5 - 1 = 4, divisible by 4.
Step 2: Assume 5^k - 1

= 4m.
Then 5^(k+1) - 1 = 5(5^k - 1) + 4 = 20m + 4, divisible by 4. (iv) Step 1: For

n = 1: 80 - 2 = 78 = 6 x 13, divisible by 6.
Step 2: Assume 8 x 10^k - 2 = 6m. Then

8 x 10^(k+1) - 2 = 10(8 x 10^k - 2) + 18 = 60m + 18, divisible by 6. (v) Step 1: For

n = 1: 1 - 1 = 0, divisible by 6.
Step 2: Assume k^3 - k = 6m.
Then (k + 1)^3 - (k +

1) = k^3 + 3k^2 + 2k = (k^3 - k) + 3k(k + 1) = 6m + 3k(k + 1); k(k + 1) is even,

so 3k(k + 1) is divisible by 6, and the sum is divisible by 6.

Q22

22. 1/3 + 1/3^2 + ... + 1/3^n = (1/2)[1 - 1/3^n]

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1/3, RHS = (1/2)(1 - 1/3) = 1/3. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is (1/2)(1 - 1/3^k).
Adding the next term 1/3^(k+1) gives (1/2)(1 -

1/3^k) + 1/3^(k+1) = 1/2 - 1/(2 x 3^k) + 1/3^(k+1) = 1/2 - 3/(2 x 3^(k+1)) + 2/(2

x 3^(k+1)) = (1/2)(1 - 1/3^(k+1)), the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q23

23. 1^2 - 2^2 + 3^2 - 4^2 + ... + (-1)^(n-1) x n^2 = (-1)^(n-1) x n(n + 1)/2

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = 1 x 2/2 = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is (-1)^(k-1) k(k + 1)/2.
Adding the next term (-1)^k (k + 1)^2 gives

(-1)^k (k + 1)[-(k/2) + (k + 1)] = (-1)^k (k + 1)(k + 2)/2, the statement for n = k +

1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q24

24. 1^3 + 3^3 + 5^3 + ... + (2n - 1)^3 = n^2[2n^2 - 1]

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = 1 x 1 = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k is k^2(2k^2 - 1).
Adding the next term (2k + 1)^3 = 8k^3 + 12k^2 +

6k + 1 gives 2k^4 - k^2 + 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 6k + 1 = 2k^4 + 8k^3 + 11k^2 + 6k

+ 1 = (k + 1)^2(2(k + 1)^2 - 1), since (k + 1)^2(2k^2 + 4k + 1) = 2k^4 + 8k^3 +

11k^2 + 6k + 1, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q25

25. x + 1 is a factor of x^(2n) - 1; (x != -1)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1), so x + 1 is a factor. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume x + 1

is a factor of x^(2k) - 1.
Then x^(2(k+1)) - 1 = x^2 x^(2k) - 1 = x^2(x^(2k) - 1) +

(x^2 - 1); both terms are divisible by x + 1, so x + 1 is a factor of x^(2k+2) - 1, the

statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q26

26. x - y is a factor of x^n - y^n; (x != y)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: x - y is a factor of x - y. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume x - y is

a factor of x^k - y^k.
Then x^(k+1) - y^(k+1) = x(x^k - y^k) + y^k(x - y); both

terms are divisible by x - y, so x - y is a factor of x^(k+1) - y^(k+1), the statement

for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q27

27. x + y is a factor of x^(2n-1) + y^(2n-1); (x != -y)

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: x + y is a factor of x + y. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume x + y is

a factor of x^(2k-1) + y^(2k-1).
Then x^(2k+1) + y^(2k+1) = x^2(x^(2k-1) +

y^(2k-1)) + y^(2k-1)(y^2 - x^2) = x^2(x^(2k-1) + y^(2k-1)) - y^(2k-1)(x - y)(x +

y); both terms are divisible by x + y, so x + y is a factor of x^(2(k+1)-1) +

y^(2(k+1)-1), the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q28

28. Use mathematical induction to show that 1 + 2 + 2^2 + ... + 2^n = 2^(n+1) -

1 for all non-negative integers n.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 0: LHS = 1, RHS = 2 - 1 = 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 1 + 2

+ ... + 2^k = 2^(k+1) - 1.
Adding the next term 2^(k+1) gives 2^(k+1) - 1 +

2^(k+1) = 2^(k+2) - 1, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q29

29. If A and B are square matrices and AB = BA, then show by mathematical

induction that AB^n = B^n A for any positive integer n.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 1: AB = BA by hypothesis. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume AB^k

= B^k A. Then AB^(k+1) = (AB^k)B = (B^k A)B = B^k(AB) = B^k(BA) =

B^(k+1)A, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Q30-31

30. Prove by the Principle of mathematical induction that n^2 - 1 is divisible by 8

when n is an odd positive integer.

Write n = 2m + 1? Induction on odd integers: for the first odd positive integer n = 1:

1 - 1 = 0, divisible by 8. Step: assume k^2 - 1 is divisible by 8 for odd k; the next

odd integer is k + 2, and (k + 2)^2 - 1 = k^2 + 4k + 3 = (k^2 - 1) + 4(k + 1); since

k is odd, k + 1 is even, so 4(k + 1) is divisible by 8; hence (k + 2)^2 - 1 is divisible

by 8. By induction on odd integers, n^2 - 1 is divisible by 8 for every odd positive

integer n.

31. Use the principle of mathematical induction to prove that ln x^n = n ln x for any

integer n >= 0 if x is a positive number.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 0: ln x^0 = ln 1 = 0 = 0 x ln x. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume ln x^k

= k ln x.
Then ln x^(k+1) = ln(x^k x x) = ln x^k + ln x = k ln x + ln x = (k + 1) ln

x, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

Use the principle of extended mathematical induction to prove that: 32. n! > 2^n -

1 for integral values of n >= 4.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 4: 4! = 24 > 15 = 2^4 - 1. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume k! >

2^k - 1 for some k >= 4.
Then (k + 1)! = (k + 1) k! > (k + 1)(2^k - 1) = (k + 1)2^k

- (k + 1).
Since (k + 1)2^k - (k + 1) >= 2^(k+1) - 1 exactly when (k - 1)2^k >= k,

which holds for k >= 4 (as 3 x 16 = 48 >= 4), we get (k + 1)! > 2^(k+1) - 1, the

statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

33. n^2 > n + 3 for integral values of n >= 3.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 3: 9 > 6. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume k^2 >

k + 3 for some k >= 3.
Then (k + 1)^2 = k^2 + 2k + 1 > k + 3 + 2k + 1 = 3k + 4

> (k + 1) + 3 = k + 4, since 3k + 4 > k + 4 for k > 0, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

34.
4^n > 3^n + 2^(n-1) for integral values of n >= 2.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 2: 16 > 9 + 2 = 11. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 4^k >

3^k + 2^(k-1) for some k >= 2.
Then 4^(k+1) = 4 x 4^k > 4(3^k + 2^(k-1)) = 4 x

3^k + 2^(k+1) = 3^(k+1) + 3^k + 2^(k+1) > 3^(k+1) + 2^k, since 3^k +

2^(k+1) > 2^k, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

35.
3^n < n! for integral values of n > 6.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 7: 3^7 = 2187 < 5040 = 7!. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 3^k <

k! for some k >= 7.
Then 3^(k+1) = 3 x 3^k < 3 x k! < (k + 1) k! = (k + 1)!, since

k + 1 > 3, the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

36. n! > n^2 for integral values of n >= 4.

Step 1 (base case): For n = 4: 24 > 16. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume k! >

k^2 for some k >= 4.
Then (k + 1)! = (k + 1) k! > (k + 1) k^2 = k^3 + k^2 > (k +

1)^2 = k^2 + 2k + 1, since k^3 > 2k + 1 for k >= 4 (64 > 9), the statement for n

= k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

37.
3 + 5 + 7 + ... + (2n + 5) = (n + 2)(n + 4) for integral values of n >= -1.

Step 1 (base case): For n = -1: the sum runs from 3 to 2(-1) + 5 = 3, so LHS = 3;

RHS = (1)(3) = 3. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume the

sum up to k (k >= -1) is (k + 2)(k + 4).
Adding the next term (2(k + 1) + 5) = 2k +

7 gives (k + 2)(k + 4) + 2k + 7 = k^2 + 6k + 8 + 2k + 7 = k^2 + 8k + 15 = (k +

3)(k + 5) = ((k + 1) + 2)((k + 1) + 4), the statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

38.
1 + nx <= (1 + x)^n for n >= 2 and x > -1 (Bernoulli's inequality).

Step 1 (base case): For n = 2: (1 + x)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2 >= 1 + 2x. True.

Step 2 (induction hypothesis): Assume the statement true for n = k. Assume 1 + kx

<= (1 + x)^k for some k >= 2.
Since x > -1, we have 1 + x > 0, so (1 + x)^(k+1)

= (1 + x)^k (1 + x) >= (1 + kx)(1 + x) = 1 + (k + 1)x + kx^2 >= 1 + (k + 1)x, the

statement for n = k + 1.

Step 3: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for every

positive integer n.

mcqs.q: By mathematical induction, 1 + 5 + 9 + ... + (4n - 3) is equal to which expression?
mcqs.why: The notes prove 1 + 5 + 9 + ... + (4n - 3) = n(2n - 1): the base case n = 1 gives 1 = 1(1), and adding the next term 4k + 1 to k(2k - 1) gives (k + 1)(2k + 1).

mcqs.q: By mathematical induction, 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1) is equal to which expression?
mcqs.why: The notes prove the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2: adding the next term 2k + 1 to k^2 gives k^2 + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)^2.

mcqs.q: By mathematical induction, 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(n-1) is equal to which expression?
mcqs.why: The notes prove 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(n-1) = 2^n - 1: adding the next term 2^k to 2^k - 1 gives 2^(k+1) - 1, completing the induction step.

mcqs.q: By mathematical induction, 1/(1x2) + 1/(2x3) + ... + 1/(n(n + 1)) is equal to which expression?
mcqs.why: The notes prove the sum equals 1 - 1/(n + 1): for n = 1 both sides are 1/2, and adding 1/((k+1)(k+2)) to k/(k+1) gives (k+1)/(k+2) = 1 - 1/(k+2).

mcqs.q: In the induction proof of 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1) = n^2, which term is added to both sides when passing from n = k to n = k + 1?
mcqs.why: The (k + 1)th odd term is 2(k + 1) - 1 = 2k + 1. Adding it gives k^2 + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)^2, as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: For the statement 1x2 + 2x3 + ... + n x (n + 1) = n(n + 1)(n + 2)/3, what value do both sides take at the base case n = 1?
mcqs.why: At n = 1 the left side is 1 x 2 = 2 and the right side is 1 x 2 x 3 / 3 = 6/3 = 2, so both sides equal 2 and the base case holds.

mcqs.q: For every positive integer n, 5^n - 1 is divisible by which number?
mcqs.why: The notes prove 5^n - 1 is divisible by 4: at n = 1, 5 - 1 = 4, and if 5^k - 1 = 4m then 5^(k+1) - 1 = 5(5^k - 1) + 4 = 20m + 4, still divisible by 4.

mcqs.q: For every positive integer n, n^3 - n is divisible by which number?
mcqs.why: The notes prove n^3 - n is divisible by 6: if k^3 - k = 6m, then (k+1)^3 - (k+1) = 6m + 3k(k+1), and k(k+1) is even so 3k(k+1) is divisible by 6.

mcqs.q: Extended mathematical induction is used to prove n! > 2^n - 1 starting from which base value of n?
mcqs.why: The base case is n = 4: 4! = 24 > 15 = 2^4 - 1. The inequality is proved for all integral values of n >= 4 by extended induction.

mcqs.q: The hockey-stick identity proved by induction states that C(3,3) + C(4,3) + ... + C(n + 2,3) is equal to which expression?
mcqs.why: The notes prove the sum equals C(n + 3,4): the base case n = 1 gives C(3,3) = 1 = C(4,4), and the step uses Pascal's identity C(m,4) + C(m,3) = C(m + 1,4).

mcqs.q: In the expansion of (a + 2b)^5, what is the coefficient of a^3 b^2 ?
mcqs.why: The term is C(5,2) a^3 (2b)^2 = 10 x a^3 x 4b^2 = 40 a^3 b^2, so the coefficient of a^3 b^2 is 40, as in the expansion given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Using the binomial theorem, what is the value of (0.97)^3 ?
Using the binomial theorem, what is the value of (21)^5 ?
What is the simplified value of (2 + sqrt(3))^5 + (2 - sqrt(3))^5 ?
What is the simplified value of (2 + i)^5 - (2 - i)^5 ?
mcqs.why: (2 + i)^5 = -38 + 41i, since (2 + i)^2 = 3 + 4i, (2 + i)^4 = -7 + 24i and (-7 + 24i)(2 + i) = -38 + 41i. Subtracting its conjugate doubles the imaginary part: 2 x 41i = 82i.

mcqs.q: What is the coefficient of x^4 in the expansion of (3 - 2x)^7 ?
mcqs.why: For x^4, r = 4 in the general term: C(7,4) x 3^3 x (-2)^4 = 35 x 27 x 16 = 15120, and the sign is positive since (-2)^4 is positive, giving 15120x^4.

mcqs.q: What is the coefficient of x^5 in the expansion of (x^2 - 3/(2x))^10 ?
mcqs.why: The general term is C(10,r)(-3/2)^r x^(20-3r). For x^5, 20 - 3r = 5 gives r = 5, so the coefficient is C(10,5)(-3/2)^5 = 252 x (-243/32) = -15309/8.

mcqs.q: What is the term independent of x in the expansion of (x - 2/x)^10 ?
mcqs.why: The general term is C(10,r)(-2)^r x^(10-2r). The constant term needs 10 - 2r = 0, so r = 5: C(10,5)(-2)^5 = 252 x (-32) = -8064.

mcqs.q: What is the term independent of x in the expansion of (1 + x^2)^3 (1 + 1/x^2)^4 ?
mcqs.why: The product equals (1 + x^2)^7 / x^8, so the constant term comes from the x^8 term of (1 + x^2)^7, which is C(7,4) = 35.

mcqs.q: What is the middle term in the expansion of (1/x - x^2/2)^12 ?
mcqs.why: There are 13 terms, so the middle term is the 7th, with r = 6: C(12,6)(1/x)^6(-x^2/2)^6 = 924 x^6/64 = 231x^6/16 after simplifying.

mcqs.q: In the expansion of (1 - x)^(1/2) up to 4 terms, what is the coefficient of x^2 ?
